# Model Routing Policy — the Haiku-first cost ladder

> **The whole point of eq-sparks.** A team of 20–50 developers gets strong, governed
> output **under budget** by defaulting to the cheapest model that can do the job and
> spending Opus only where human-grade judgment is genuinely required. This document is
> the cost centrepiece: it decides *which model each agent runs on* and *when — and only
> when — it is allowed to cost more*.

Three rungs, mapped 1:1 onto the Claude Code `model:` tiers an agent declares in its
frontmatter. **Cheaper is the default; escalation is the exception and must be earned.**

---

## The three rungs

### Rung 1 — HAIKU (cheap & fast)
Mechanical, well-scoped, rule-based work. No design judgment, no ambiguity, deterministic
"does it match the rule?" output. This is where the **majority of calls should land**.

- **Agents:** `@scanner`, `@tester`, `@docs`, `@a11y`
- **Skills:** `ado-context`, `figma-context`, the `dna-precheck` scan pass, `console-render`
- **Why Haiku is enough:** the work is pattern-matching, fetching, formatting, or running
  a fixed checklist (lint output, dependency diff, secret regex, WCAG aria/contrast/focus
  rules, XML/JSDoc updates, running a test and reading the result). The "thinking" lives
  in the rules, not the model.

### Rung 2 — SONNET (mid: the workhorse)
Code generation and most specialist reasoning. Needs to read context, produce or edit
real code, and reason inside one well-defined domain — but is **not** making cross-cutting
governance calls.

- **Core agents:** `@codegen`, `@reviewer`, `@perf`, `@integration-tester`, `@contract-tester`
- **Frontend specialists:** `@mfe`, `@shared-curator`, `@design-system`, `@state`, `@contract`
- **BFF specialists:** `@domain-folder`, `@bff-shaper`, `@downstream-connector`, `@contract-publisher`
- **Why Sonnet:** these agents write code and apply EQ conventions/patterns within a
  bounded scope. Strong enough to be correct; far cheaper than Opus per call, and they run
  *per file / per module*, so per-call cost compounds — Sonnet keeps that compounding cheap.

### Rung 3 — OPUS (rare: judgment, planning, adversarial review)
Hard, cross-cutting judgment that decides the shape of the whole run or blocks it. Used
**sparingly — once per stage, not per file.**

- **Agents:** `@supervisor`, `@decision`, `@critic`, `@architect`, `@security`
- **Why Opus:** planning + budget allocation, ambiguity resolution, strict adversarial
  PASS/FAIL gating, where-does-code-belong decomposition, and threat reasoning are exactly
  the calls where a wrong cheap answer is expensive downstream. These ~5 agents are the
  only ones that touch Opus by default, and they are invoked at stage boundaries — not on
  every artifact — so Opus stays a thin slice of total spend.

---

## The rule: start at your default tier

**Every agent starts at the tier declared in its own frontmatter `model:` field.** That
default tier is authoritative; it is reproduced in the table below. No agent silently
runs on a different model. The default is the cheapest model that the agent's scope is
expected to handle.

---

## Confidence-gated escalation (one rung, earned, logged)

An agent may run **one rung hotter** — and only one — when **either** trigger fires:

1. **(a) Low self-eval confidence.** The mandatory `self-evaluate` step before hand-off
   returns **confidence < 0.7 on any criterion**. The agent could not convince itself it
   met the bar.
2. **(b) Repeated critic FAIL.** `@critic` returns **FAIL on the same worker twice** for
   the same task. The cheap rung has demonstrably failed the quality gate.

Rules around escalation:

- **One rung only.** Haiku → Sonnet, or Sonnet → Opus. Never two rungs in one jump. If a
  Haiku agent escalates to Sonnet and *still* trips a trigger, that is an `@architect` /
  `@decision` problem (wrong agent or unclear PBI), not a reason to vault to Opus.
- **Requested from `@supervisor`.** The worker does not self-promote. It raises an
  escalation request; `@supervisor` approves against remaining budget (see
  **budget-policy**) and records the decision.
- **Logged.** Every escalation is written to the run log with: agent id, trigger ((a) or
  (b)), the failing criterion / critic finding, the from→to tiers, and the approving
  `@supervisor` call. This is auditable by humans.
- **Charged to the budget.** The hotter call's tokens count against the run ceiling. An
  escalation that would breach the ceiling is denied; `@supervisor` makes the go/no-go
  call instead (see **budget-policy**).
- **NEVER auto-downgrade mid-task.** A task that has been escalated stays escalated until
  it completes and hands off. We do not flip-flop tiers within a task — that wastes the
  prompt-cache prefix (see **cache-policy**) and risks inconsistent output. The next
  *fresh* task starts again at the agent's default tier.

---

## Escalation never replaces caching or dedup

Before paying for a hotter model, the platform must already have avoided paying for repeat
work at all:

- **cache-policy** — fetch/scan agents (`@scanner`, plus `ado-context` / `figma-context`)
  hit the cache first; cached skill output and the stable Anthropic prompt-cache prefix
  (`[platform | agent spec | volatile task]`, 5-min TTL) mean we are not re-paying for the
  same tokens. Escalation only ever applies to *new, low-confidence* work.
- **dedup-policy** — build agents run `dna-precheck` first (REUSE > EXTEND > CREATE) and
  the task ledger lets resumes skip done work. The cheapest token is the one we never
  spend because we reused existing code.

Escalation is the *last* lever, after cache and dedup have already done their job.

---

## Agent → default tier → escalation trigger

| Agent | Layer | Default tier | Escalation trigger (one rung only) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@supervisor` | governance | **opus** | Top rung — does not escalate. Owns escalation approvals for others. |
| `@decision` | governance | **opus** | Top rung — no further escalation. |
| `@critic` | governance | **opus** | Top rung — no further escalation. |
| `@architect` | core | **opus** | Top rung — no further escalation. |
| `@security` | core | **opus** | Top rung — no further escalation. |
| `@codegen` | core | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@reviewer` | core | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@perf` | core | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@integration-tester` | core | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@contract-tester` | core | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@mfe` | frontend | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@shared-curator` | frontend | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@design-system` | frontend | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@state` | frontend | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@contract` | frontend | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@domain-folder` | bff | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@bff-shaper` | bff | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@downstream-connector` | bff | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@contract-publisher` | bff | **sonnet** | → opus on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@tester` | core | **haiku** | → sonnet on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@scanner` | core | **haiku** | → sonnet on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@docs` | core | **haiku** | → sonnet on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |
| `@a11y` | frontend | **haiku** | → sonnet on self-eval < 0.7 **or** 2× `@critic` FAIL |

**Tally:** 5 opus (governance trio + `@architect` + `@security`), 14 sonnet, 4 haiku
defaults across the 23-agent roster — plus the Haiku-tier skills (`ado-context`,
`figma-context`, the `dna-precheck` scan, `console-render`).

## Worked cost example — a typical `/scaffold` run

A representative `/scaffold` of one ADO PBI that adds a screen to a child MFE and a new
BFF domain folder. Counting **calls** (one invocation each), not raw tokens:

| Stage | Calls on Haiku | Calls on Sonnet | Calls on Opus |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intake — `ado-context`, `figma-context`, `dna-precheck` scan | 4 | — | — |
| Plan & budget — `@supervisor`, `@architect`, `@decision` (once each) | — | — | 3 |
| Build — `@mfe`, `@design-system`, `@state`, `@contract`, `@domain-folder`, `@bff-shaper`, `@downstream-connector`, `@contract-publisher`, `@codegen` (per file) | — | 12 | — |
| Verify — `@tester`, `@scanner`, `@a11y`, `@docs` | 9 | — | — |
| Specialist review — `@reviewer`, `@perf`, `@integration-tester`, `@contract-tester` | — | 5 | — |
| Govern — `@security` (once), `@critic` (once per stage gate) | — | — | 4 |
| Render — `console-render` | 2 | — | — |
| **Totals** | **15** | **17** | **7** |

- **Haiku + Sonnet = 32 of 39 calls ≈ 82%** of the run lands on the two cheap rungs.
- **Opus = 7 of 39 ≈ 18%**, and those are the **~5 opus agents invoked once per stage**
  (plan, security pass, and the critic gate between stages) — **never per file**. The 12
  per-file build calls and 9 verify calls — the high-volume, repetitive work — stay on
  Sonnet and Haiku.
- If, say, `@codegen` self-evaluates at 0.6 on correctness for one file, that **single**
  file's call escalates Sonnet → Opus (logged, budget-charged). The other 11 build calls
  are untouched. Escalation is surgical, not a tier-wide flip.

**This is how the team gets good output cheaply.** Defaulting to Haiku/Sonnet, reusing
the cache (**cache-policy**) and dedup ledger (**dedup-policy**), and reserving Opus for
the ~5 judgment agents at stage boundaries means the platform leans hard on the cheap
models for ~80%+ of the work while the strict `@critic` + confidence-gated escalation keep
quality from sagging. Cheap by default; expensive only when it's earned and logged.
